articles.title: Who are Mirra Andreeva’s parents? The family story behind the 2026 French Open finalist’s success
articles.summary: International Sports News: At just 19 years old, Mirra Andreeva has become one of the biggest young names in tennis. The Russian star reached her first Grand Slam final at the 2.
articles.body: At just 19 years old, Mirra Andreeva has become one of the biggest young names in tennis. The Russian star reached her first Grand Slam final at the 2026 French Open and has already climbed into the world’s top five. Her fast rise has made fans curious not only about her tennis journey but also about the family that helped her get there. Behind many of Mirra Andreeva’s biggest moments are her parents, Raisa Andreeva and Alexander Andreev. They played a major role in helping both Mirra and her older sister, Erika Andreeva, build careers in professional tennis. While Mirra now competes on the sport’s biggest stages, her journey began years ago with a family decision that changed everything.According to Town & Country magazine, Mirra’s parents carefully considered different sports for their daughters before choosing tennis. That choice helped set the foundation for one of the brightest young careers in the game today.How Raisa Andreeva and Alexander Andreev helped shape Mirra Andreeva’s tennis journey?Mirra Andreeva has often credited her mother, Raisa Andreeva, for introducing her to tennis. Speaking on the Tennis Insider Club podcast in 2025, Mirra explained that her parents once discussed whether she and Erika should play tennis or volleyball.“My mum told us when she was pregnant with Erika she would wake up at night to watch some tennis matches and some volleyball matches,” Mirra said.As a young child, Mirra spent much of her time around tennis courts. The future star said she was barely old enough to hold a racket when she first tried to play.“I think since I was like two-years-old I have spent a lot of time on a tennis court,” she recalled. “I tried to play since I was like four, but I was so small and I couldn’t hold the tennis racket in my hand.”Mirra also joked that tennis was not completely her own choice in the beginning.“It was not my choice, they kind of forced me,” she said while laughing.While Raisa has regularly been seen supporting her daughter at tournaments, Mirra’s father, Alexander Andreev, has mostly stayed out of public view. Town & Country reported that he helped oversee financial matters and career earnings before Mirra turned 18.That support has helped Mirra focus on her game as she continues to achieve major milestones. She became a WTA 1000 champion at 17, broke into the world’s top 10 at a young age, and has earned more than $2.1 million in career prize money, according to her official WTA profile. With her parents guiding her from the start, Mirra continues to build one of tennis’ most exciting success stories.

articles.title: US Open: No. 3 Jessica Pegula survives rough start vs. Emma Navarro to set up clash with No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka
articles.summary: Pegula and Sabalenka are both in contention for the WTA No. 1 ranking.
articles.body:
Jessica Pegula didn't exactly play like the No. 3 player in the world on Tuesday, but she's still alive at the US Open.

The top-seeded American in the field overcame an awful start in the quarterfinals to defeat No. 26 seed and countrywoman Emma Navarro 3-6, 6-4, 6-3. Her reward will be a matchup with No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka on Thursday, in the latter's third straight US Open semifinal.

Pegula will have to overcome history to go further. Sabalenka ended both of those runs, with a straight-sets win in the 2024 final and a three-set thriller in last year's semifinal. Sabalenka leads their career head-to-head 9-4, though Pegula won their most recent meeting 6-4, 6-7, 6-0 in Berlin earlier this year.

Both Sabalenka and Pegula remain in contention for the WTA's No. 1 ranking coming out of the tournament, though all of that goes up in smoke if No. 2 Elena Rybakina wins her quarterfinal match against Qinwen Zheng on Wednesday.

If Rybakina does lose, she still becomes No. 1 unless Pegula, Sabalenka or Coco Gauff win the title. Like Pegula, Sabalenka took a major step toward that goal on Tuesday with an intense three-set win over No. 6 seed Linda Noskova .

Jessica Pegula clearly frustrated in first set

Pegula had to do plenty of work just to keep her hopes alive. Facing a fellow daughter of a billionaire family — the jokes are too easy to bother with — she was inexplicably tight in the first set.

Her serve was particularly rough early on. She rarely got her first serve in, landing only 11 of 28 in her first three service games. Her second serve was easy to abuse when it actually landed, winning only 6-of-17 points on it while committing five double faults in those same three games. Navarro, who entered the match with an 0-4 record against Pegula, wasn't at her best either, but she kept it together enough to cruise to a first set win.

Even baseline rallies, the area where Pegula is supposed to be one of the steadiest players on tour, weren't going her way, with a noticeably low ball-striking angle resulting in countless balls landing in the net.

Pegula was aware of her issues. She bounced her racket against the court in frustration at one point and ESPN cameras caught her telling her coaches that she has never double-faulted so many times in her life. Even her own coach Mark Knowles told ESPN she was playing too passively between sets.

"I wasn't exactly serving my best and I was fighting a lot of demons out there today," Pegula said in her post-match interview.

She got moderately better in the second set, but still had to dig deep to avoid a straight-sets loss. A late break allowed her to steal the set and stay alive.

Pegula's main adjustment appeared to be ramping down her serve velocity and trusting her baseline game. It worked, even if she still had to respond to a break by Navarro that put her down 2-1 in the third set. She did so by winning the next four games, cruising to a win that took a surprising amount of fortitude.

It's been a career season for Pegula, who leads the WTA in wins this year with 50, but what she would like most of all is a Grand Slam title. Every other player in the top 6, from Sabalenka to Noskova, has won one of the four trophies all players covet.

With her biggest success coming on hard court and friendly crowds at Flushing Meadows, the US Open has always loomed as her best shot at breaking through. She's two matches from accomplishing that, but the degree of difficulty is already looking like it will be very high.

articles.title: US Open: Frances Tiafoe consoles heartbroken Alex Michelsen after wild comeback
articles.summary: Frances Tiafoe pulled off the biggest comeback of the US Open. Then he helped produce one of the best moments of the US Open.
articles.body:
Frances Tiafoe pulled off the biggest comeback of the US Open. Then he helped produce one of the best moments of the US Open.

Following his thrilling, five-set comeback against Alex Michelsen , Tiafoe shared an embrace with his good friend and countryman after giving him the most painful loss of his career. Michelsen was clearly crying and left the court with a towel over his head.

Michelsen had the match in hand in the third set, holding a 7-5, 6-3, 5-3 lead at one point. He was serving for the set when he opened the game with back-to-back double-faults, giving Tiafoe all the runway he needed to get back in the match.

The 22-year-old Michelsen also was up a break in the fifth set but gave it back and eventually lost in a 10-point tiebreaker. It was the first Grand Slam quarterfinal of his career, and it ended as painfully as possible.

His embrace with Tiafoe quickly started going viral after the match, with Tiafoe sharing his perspective in an ESPN interview:

"As soon as I hugged him, I seen that he was crying already, I was like, 'Man I know. I've been there. I've been there twice, to be fair ... He's young, he hasn't been there. We're super-tight. We laugh and joke all the time, one of my good buddies on tour. I know how much that hurts. I know how much he wanted it today. It's something that you dream about. "I just told him, 'Bro, I know you're going to be here so many more times. I'm going to be in a rocking chair when you do so.'"

"As soon as I hugged him, I seen that he was crying already, I was like, 'Man I know. I've been there. I've been there twice, to be fair ... He's young, he hasn't been there. We're super-tight. We laugh and joke all the time, one of my good buddies on tour. I know how much that hurts. I know how much he wanted it today. It's something that you dream about.

"I just told him, 'Bro, I know you're going to be here so many more times. I'm going to be in a rocking chair when you do so.'"

Tiafoe is one of the most popular players on tour for a reason. In addition to being an exciting player who always seems to deliver in New York City, he is beloved among his peers. Michelsen certainly seemed to appreciate him while speaking with reporters after the match:

"I wasn't saying much, I was trying to keep it together and didn't do a good job of that. He was saying a lot of nice, personal things, 'You'll be there,' when I'm older. 'You're gonna be here. We're going to play again.' He's a great guy for consoling me in that moment."

Tiafoe will face another fellow American, No. 8 Ben Shelton, on Friday, after Shelton's late-night epic against Carlos Alcaraz .

articles.title: Tennis: Meet the doubles team with a 66-year age gap
articles.summary: David McCandless, 80, and his 14-year-old doubles partner Liam teamed up two years ago – and they haven't looked back since.
articles.body:
They may be 66 years apart in age, but on the tennis court David McCandless and his doubles partner Liam have developed a partnership that has proved a winning combination.

The 80-year-old and his 14-year-old counterpart teamed up two years ago and have not looked back since.

Since then, the unlikely pairing have won more than half of their North West of Ireland league games - after ironing out a few kinks.

"We started on court and it was a case of who is going to go where," Liam said. "Then after a couple of matches we started winning because we realised we got a system down and we realised we are a pretty good duo."

David said the partnership came about "purely by accident" but two years later it had "worked out very well indeed".

"He's a very strong young junior and I think he will be a top class player," he said.

David was the same age as his partner when he first took up tennis and has loved every minute of his time on court, now playing up to four or five times a week.

He believes the experience he has gained over the years can complement Liam's coaching and natural ability.

"He got coaching from a young age which I never got," David said. "I wouldn't have the same ability in playing the correct shots. I'm just self-taught."

"I do have a bit of experience and I do think that I can help him as regards how to move on the court at times," he continued.

"And he knows what I'm capable of and he covers for me at other times."

Liam is equally complimentary about his older partner, saying he brings a lot of experience to the court.

"He's a solid player and consistent and I've learned a lot from him playing in the league," he said.

The pair are part of City of Derry Tennis Club, which now has about 100 members despite not having a clubhouse or courts of its own.

The club said its membership included people of all ages and backgrounds from across the community.

"That's something we pride ourselves on," club spokesman Keith Bloomfield said.

"We have a great cross community and cross border club and we have many foreign nationals now taking up the game - from India, Ukraine, and Malaysia amongst others."

And for those involved, tennis is about much more than winning matches.

Coach Catherine Gallen said the sport had become an important outlet for her.

"It's just so good for your physical and mental health," she said. "Like I'd come back from school and play tennis and it's just such a release.

"I've made so many friends from tennis. It's just so sociable."

"If you've had a tough day or you are going through something difficult just to get out there and hit those balls it's a fantastic release," she said.

But despite the club going from strength to strength, it faces a significant problem - it has no home of its own and has to rent different courts around Derry.

For decades, the tennis courts at St Columb's Park were regarded as the home of tennis in the city - and the club would like to see the site restored to its former glory.

"It is a great shame that such a beautiful and iconic facility cannot be restored," Bloomfield added. "What will happen to those courts?"

He said funding for repairing and upgrading the courts was not included in any council capital plans - and the club believes other towns have facilities that Derry is lacking.

"Neighbouring towns have bespoke clubs and clubhouses and facilities and it's a pity that a city the size of Derry doesn't have such a facility of its own," Bloomfield said.

Over the last two years, club representatives have met with council staff to discuss facilities for tennis in the city.

A spokesperson for Derry City and Strabane District Council said it recognised "the value of tennis and the very positive contribution local clubs make to the sport".

They said the council was aware of concerns regarding some facilities and representatives had met with the club to discuss ways to address them, and with Tennis Ireland and Sport NI to explore funding opportunities to upgrade existing courts.

"It is council's assessment that there is currently adequate provision for tennis across the city, based on existing capacity, usage levels and booking demands across available facilities," the spokesperson added.

The club said that, on paper, there were enough courts in the city - there are four at Waterside Shared Village, six at St Columb's Park and two at Clooney Park West, but the reality is a different story.

The St Columb's Park courts have been closed to the public throughout the summer pending a safety assessment, while the tarmac courts at Clooney Park are also said to be in poor condition.

That leaves the courts at Waterside Shared Village, where, the club said, even the line markings are showing their age.

For David and Liam, their unlikely partnership is a small example of what tennis can offer - regardless of age.

articles.title: Tennis: Naomi Osaka makes passionate defence of on-court outfits at US Open
articles.summary: Naomi Osaka says any criticism she receives for her outfits is "worth it" if it means "the people after me have an easier path".
articles.body:
Naomi Osaka says any criticism she receives for her extravagant outfits is "worth it" if it means "the people after me have an easier path".

The 28-year-old is renowned for her eye-catching on-court attire, which included a hooded white gown for her first-round win against Anastasia Zakharova at the US Open.

Underneath was an all-black basketball-style kit in which Osaka played, while she also had her hair braided and wore a headband in a tribute to former NBA star Allen Iverson, who she called a "trailblazer" as "he's kind of like done a lot in fashion, whether it's on purpose or not".

In her latest outfit, Japan's four-time Grand Slam champion wore a decorated coat at the start of her last-16 US Open defeat by Elena Rybakina.

In defending her fashion statements, she referred to speaking out about her mental health in 2021 when she refused to speak to the media at the French Open and subsequently withdrew from the tournament.

Osaka, whose father is Haitian-American and mother is Japanese, also highlighted her ancestry.

"I don't mind being the first to do something and getting trashed for it," she wrote in a social media post.

"This happened when I talked about mental health and for some reason it's happening with my clothes lol.

"I'm literally Haitian it's in my blood to be this way, as long as the people after me have an easier path it's worth it."

articles.title: US Open: Ben Shelton powers through Carlos Alcaraz in historic, late-night thriller
articles.summary: Ben Shelton will face Frances Tiafoe in the semifinal, after the biggest win of his career.
articles.body:
The US Open men's final is guaranteed to feature a single American, courtesy of the biggest win, and latest night, of Ben Shelton's career.

In the final hour of Tuesday and the early hours of Wednesday, the No. 8 seed defeated defending champion Carlos Alcaraz 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 in a Match of the Year candidate between two of the sport's young stars.

With the final shot landing at 3:33 a.m., the four-and-a-half-hour match featured the latest ending in US Open history, surpassing Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner's legendary clash in the 2022 quarterfinals (2:50 a.m.). The match ended so late that the cleaners started working inside Ashe in the fifth set .

Shelton's reward will be an All-American match against No. 11 seed Frances Tiafoe in the semifinal on Friday. Whoever wins will become only the second American man to reach the US Open in final in the past two decades (Taylor Fritz, 2024), looking to end a Grand Slam drought that goes back to Andy Roddick's US Open title in 2003.

Shelton did it against a seven-time Grand Slam champion who, to be fair, was also playing his first tournament in more than four months. Alcaraz had little trouble reaching the quarterfinals, dropping only one set in four matches, but Shelton always represented a different difficulty level, against whom Alcaraz would have to be fully functional.

Entering the match, Alcaraz was 14-0 in Grand Slams against Americans and 13-0 against left-handers. He had won 12 straight five-set matches and 18 overall. Shelton ended all of those streaks, picking up his first career Grand Slam win over a top-five player in the process.

Carlos Alcaraz-Ben Shelton lived up to the hype, for those who stayed up

From the moment the draw was revealed, this particular quarterfinal matchup was tantalizing for tennis fans. The pair are two of the hardest-hitting, quickest-moving, loudest-shouting, all-court players on tour. Entertainers, in addition to being elite tennis players at 23 years old.

It was the perfect showcase for modern tennis, so naturally the US Open's comically flawed schedule forced them to begin the proceedings around 11 p.m. local time. The first three matches at Arthur Ashe Stadium were all thrillers that went the distance, so fans at least got their money's worth.

Alcaraz-Shelton was worth staying up for. There was Shelton unleashing serves up to 150 mph and throwing down jumping volleys. There was Alcaraz reaching balls no other player is capable of touching. One such point:

The match began on even footing, with the pair staying on serve in the first set until it was 5-5, at which point they exchanged breaks to force a tiebreaker. Shelton led that at 5-3, only for Alcaraz to roar back with four straight points.

Alcaraz started the second set with a 14-point hold then similarly pushed Shelton's subsequent service game, but it was after that point something seemed to give.

There are plenty of possible explanations for why Alcaraz lost the next nine consecutive games. He could have felt something in his wrist and become more tentative. He could have tweaked something on an awkward jumping volley in that Shelton service game. He could have finally felt the exhaustion of playing his best opponent since losing to Jannik Sinner at Monte Carlo on April 12. He could have been saving energy for what was clearly to come.

Whatever happened, Alcaraz didn't move the way he usually does and committed an inordinate amount of unforced errors with a forehand that is usually among the best in tennis. He was a full step behind Shelton for a set and a half, only making things competitive in a third set where he couldn't get the necessary break to take back momentum.

It was a career-best effort by Shelton, who also showed a more reserved demeanor as the match went on and the possibility of an upset became more real. Shelton has always run hot and cold as a player, sometimes to his detriment, but his only reaction to his third-set win was a satisfied stare at his coach's box .

Alcaraz, of course, started feeling better, or at least started performing better. He got a break on his first opportunity in the fourth set and pressed that advantage into forcing the fifth set.

Along the way, he was seen heaving into his towel on a changeover . That was also around the time ESPN cameras caught new USTA president Craig Tiley appearing on the verge of falling asleep because, again, these guys were playing a match at an hour and length that would match a cross-country red-eye flight.

As the clock reached and then passed 3 a.m., the two men locked in for the most intense set of the match. Both faced break points in the fifth set, both saved them all. Shelton started emptying his emotional tank while Alcaraz looked increasingly at home, powered by the adrenaline that has made him nearly unbeatable in five-set matches.

It all came down to that final, 10-point tiebreaker. Shelton got it done, ending it all with a 146-mph ace.

articles.title: Alcaraz cede la corona de Nueva York en el súper 'tie break' ante Shelton
articles.standfirst: El duelo entre Ben y Tiafoe asegura la presencia de un estadounidense en la final del domingo
articles.summary: El duelo entre Ben y Tiafoe asegura la presencia de un estadounidense en la final del domingo
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz no se ha podido clasificar por cuarta vez en su carrera para las semifinales del Abierto de los Estados Unidos tras caer con el local Ben Shelton, por 5-7(5), 6-1, 6-3 y 7-6(7), en 4 horas y 28 minutos. Era apenas la segunda derrota de Alcaraz a cinco sets en 17 partidos, lo que enseña la dimensión del triunfo de Ben. El partido se inició a las 23.00 horas del martes en Nueva York después de las 2 horas y 20 minutos que se alargó el duelo de cuartos entre Jessica Pegula y Emma Navarro. Terminó a las 03.35 de la madrugada. La pista Arthur Ashe, la más grande del planeta tenis, se mantuvo llena para seguir el espectáculo ofrecido por Alcaraz y Shelton. "Ha sido un honor compartir la pista con Carlos", dijo el ganador a la conclusión. Ben estuvo en la pelea gracias a la inspiración con el servicio. Alcanzó puntas de 234 kilómetros por hora. Carlitos dio primero con un 'break' en el undécimo juego y sacó después para adelantarse en el marcador. Un par de derechas mal tocadas llevaron el desenlace a la muerte súbita. Alcaraz fue mejor a siete puntos y resoplaba porque el americano se había anotado el punto del torneo, en el 1-1. Shelton, que jugaba en casa, no iba a rendirse tan fácilmente y logró una doble segunda rotura para situar un tanteo favorable de 3-1 en la continuación. En el palco de Ben aplaudía su pareja, la estrella del fútbol americano Trinity Rodman. Con empate a una manga todo empezaba de cero. Era como jugar un partido del circuito ATP al mejor de tres sets. El cansancio, sin embargo, hacía más mella en el tenista con menos rodaje. Y ese era Alcaraz. Los 139 días sin competir se notaban, en especial en la puesta en escena de la pelota. Dos de los tres breaks concedidos en el segundo set habían sido con doble falta. Había decantado a su favor el 45 por ciento de los puntos con segundo saque. Ya eran ocho los juegos seguidos sumados por Shelton. Al pupilo de Samuel López también le penalizaba el 1/6 en pelotas de rotura. Atajó la sangría de juegos en contra con el 3-1. Lo que pasa es que el saque del americano no le dio opción para intentar remontar la tercera manga. Carlitos sufría desajustes en sus tiros propios del largo parón por la lesión en la muñeca derecha. El casillero de errores no forzados se disparaba hasta los 35. Alcaraz se agarró al cemento y buscó reengancharse al partido con una pelota de 5-4. El estadounidense la salvó a raquetazo limpio y suyo fue el tercer set. El murciano demostró toda su grandeza forzando el desempate cuando pocos le daban opción por su lenguaje corporal, con claros signos de cansancio. Shelton estaba ofuscado y no veía portería. Fue por ello que se marchó a los vestuarios para intentar cambiar el ritmo y la dinámica del partido. "Que te vea", le insistía Samuel a su pupilo. Los aficionados yanquis de la Arthur Ashe empezaron a gritar "USA, USA...". No era un partido de Copa Davis. El ruido en la central más grande del mundo llegaba a ser ensordecedor. A Ben se le escaparon tres pelotas de 5-3 porque su oponente le puso cabeza, corazón y cojones", el lema de su abuelo. "Let's go", soltaba el vigente campeón. Shelton se aseguró el súper 'tie break' y mandó toda la presión al otro lado de la red. Suyo fue finalmente el triunfo en el cara o cruz. Su servicio marcó la diferencia. La victoria del americano garantiza la presencia de un tenista local en la final del domingo. Y es que el verdugo de Alcaraz se cruzará este viernes con su compatriota Frances Tiafoe. El US Open se queda sin Carlitos y la grada sin sus celebtaciones.

articles.title: Ben Shelton beats Carlos Alcaraz in latest ever U.S. Open finish
articles.summary: There’s leaving it late, and then there’s what Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz just served up at the U.S.
articles.body: There’s leaving it late, and then there’s what Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz just served up at the U.S. Open. The American star ultimately outdueled the defending champion in the latest ever finish at the tournament, a thriller that didn’t finish until 3:33 a.m. in front of a raucous New York crowd. The five-set victory takes Shelton to the semifinals, where he will face fellow American Frances Tiafoe. That means there is guaranteed to be an American in Sunday’s final, hoping to end a drought that has seen no U.S. men’s player win a Grand Slam since Andy Roddick in New York in 2003. Shelton, the No. 8 seed, ended Alcaraz’ 18-match winning streak in Grand Slam tournaments in a clash that lasted 4 hours, 28 minutes. At one point, the Spaniard could be seen vomiting into a towel. The grueling quarterfinal was played under the lights after a day of marathon contests at Flushing Meadows. The highlight-filled match swung back and forth, with Shelton winning the second and third sets after losing the first on a tie break. No. 2 seed Alcaraz, who missed most of the season with a wrist injury, won the fourth set 6-1 to set up a grueling final set. The pair traded blows but ultimately couldn’t be separated until the final set tiebreaker, which Shelton won 10-7. The epic now stands as the latest finish in the history of a tournament increasingly known for its overnight duels. That honor had previously been held by another Alcaraz match, against his rival at the top of the sport Jannik Sinner, which finished at 2:50 a.m in the 2022 quarterfinals. That victory helped Alcaraz, then 19, on the way to his first U.S. Open title. He’ll now set his sights on regaining the form that made him the sport’s leading light. Three of Tuesday’s four singles quarterfinal matches went to match tiebreakers, the day starting with Aryna Sabalenka edging Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova to keep alive her hopes of a third straight U.S. title. Tiafoe then outlasted fellow American Alex Michelsen, staging repeated comebacks to set up the semifinal with Shelton. Thousands of fans stayed to the gripping end, with both Shelton and the popular showman Alcaraz enjoying loud support in Arthur Ashe Stadium. “It’s incredible,” Shelton said. “I always say that this is the greatest sports city in the world, I say that this is the greatest stadium in the world. I’m just hoping that my best friend and my sister over there don’t have to be at work at 6 a.m. in three hours.” Alcaraz said he could “leave the court happy,” and the seven-time Grand Slam champion offered praise for his American opponent. “I leave the court with a smile. I am proud of myself, how I fought,” he said. “Shelton played a very complete, very mature match,” Alcaraz added in Spanish. “He knew exactly what to do at every moment. And, physically, he’s a beast. It seemed like he had no weaknesses whatsoever.” Shelton summed up the evening. “It was a war,” he said. articles.title: Lo que le queda a Carlos Alcaraz: seis torneos seguros y uno más si España está en la final de la Copa Davis
articles.standfirst: El español regresa a España y no volverá a competir hasta el 25 de septiembre en la Laver Cup
articles.summary: El español regresa a España y no volverá a competir hasta el 25 de septiembre en la Laver Cup
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz, tras caer eliminado en los cuartos del US Open a manos de Ben Shelton, terminando una racha de 18 victorias en los grandes, regresa a España. Descansará unos días antes de preparar su vuelta a la competición, que será en la Laver Cup 2026 (25 al 27). La novena edición del torneo ideado en su día por Roger Federer se celebrará en el O2 de Londres. Es la segunda vez que Europa y el Resto del Mundo se medirán en la capital británica. Hace cuatro años fue allí la retirada oficial de Federer en un histórico dobles con Rafael Nadal que acabaron perdiendo con los americanos Frances Tiafoe y Jack Sock. El pupilo de Samuel López, con un increíble tirón popular, se ha convertido en un fijo en la Laver Cup. Es su tercera presencia seguida. En 2024 lideró al equipo europeo a la victoria en Berlín. Alcaraz volará directamente de Londres a Tokio para defender la corona del torneo de categoría 500 (30 de septiembre al 6 de octubre). articles.body: Mientras Ben Shelton se ejercitaba el lunes en las pistas de Flushing Meadows, los aficionados buscaban a Carlos Alcaraz, un ídolo de masas en Nueva York y en cualquier punto del planeta al que viaja. El murciano decidió, junto a los miembros de su equipo, tomarse el día libre para ser un turista más en la ciudad de los rascacielos. Junto a su cuerpo técnico se desplazó al parque de Chelsea para estirar los músculos y conocer un enclave que destaca por la estatua Chelsea Doughboy: Dentro del propio parque, en el lateral de la Novena Avenida, se puede ver este histórico monumento de bronce de 1921 dedicado a los soldados locales de la Primera Guerra Mundial. Alcaraz también ha visitado el nuevo parque flotante. Alexander Zverev, primer cabeza de serie del cuadro individual masculino, ha jugado cuatro partidos y todos ellos han sido en el último turno de la sesión nocturna. Y lo mismo pasará este miércoles con el quinto, en los cuartos que le cruzarán ante Botic van de Zandschulp. Mientras la mayoría de jugadores prefieren evitar la sesión nocturna, para tener la tarde libre e irse antes a dormir. Zverev prioriza el sueño. En los Grand Slam, ha confesado que necesita entre 10 y 11 horas, y no le gusta madrugar. Solución: jugar de noche cuando nadie más quiere. Eso le permite librarse de las ruedas de prensa oficiales y se limita a dar un par de declaraciones en una especie de zona mixta. Wimbledon ha dicho basta a la corriente de poblar los torneos de 'influencers' con millones de seguidores en sus redes sociales, pero sin conocimiento de tenis. En Estados Unidos todo es a lo grande. Alcaraz no sólo destaca en la pista sino también con su banquillo. Al igual que el tenista, sus hombres de confianza tienen varias equipaciones estos días en Nueva York. Shelton ganó el partido de cuartos gracias a la poderosa arma que tiene en el servicio. En el segundo punto del partido fue capaz de mandar la pelota a 233 kilómetros por hora. articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Carlos Alcaraz beaten by Ben Shelton in epic quarter-final
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence is over after a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton which ends at 03:34 local time.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz's US Open title defence came to an end in a dramatic five-set quarter-final loss to Ben Shelton which ended at 03:34 local time - the latest finish in the tournament's history.

A large crowd remained captivated deep into the night as a modern classic unfolded over an unpredictable four hours and 28 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

The match did not begin until about 11pm in New York, after the start of the night session was delayed by Tuesday's earlier matches.

At its conclusion, eighth seed Shelton basked in a standing ovation from a delirious audience after completing a 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) victory that will live long in the memory of all those present.

"That was a war, an epic match, so physical," Shelton said.

"Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old.

"It's ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes - the most enjoyable match that I've had in my career, for sure."

This was the biggest - and certainly most significant - win of Shelton's career.

He had not beaten a top-three player in 17 attempts, and had lost each of his three previous matches against Spain's Alcaraz.

It also boosted home hopes of a first American men's singles champion in New York for 23 years.

Shelton was less than a year old when Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003 - but an American finalist is guaranteed when he and Frances Tiafoe meet in Friday's semi-finals.

World number three Alcaraz was competing at his first tournament since a lengthy injury lay-off, but that is to take nothing away from Shelton, who produced a phenomenal performance.

Seven-time major winner Alcaraz had exceeded expectations on his return after more than four months out with a wrist injury, including sweeping past 20th seed Tommy Paul to reach the last eight.

But the 23-year-old's lack of match fitness appeared to finally catch up with him in a high-octane encounter filled with breathless exchanges and astounding displays of athleticism.

Even when it appeared Alcaraz had emptied the tank, the two-time winner not only forced a deciding set but would go the distance as the players engaged in a tense 10-point match tie-break that provided a fitting conclusion to the contest.

"It was close. So I'm just not going to be disappointed about not getting the win at the end," said Alcaraz.

"I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought. I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed."

While home hope Shelton had the vast support of the hardy crowd, Alcaraz has always felt at home at Flushing Meadows.

The Spaniard had won 28 of his 31 matches at the tournament - the highest win rate at the US Open in the sport's professional era at above 90% - and last year became the first man to reach the final without dropping a set since Roger Federer in 2015.

The Australian Open champion was also on an 18-match unbeaten streak at Grand Slam tournaments, having missed the French Open and Wimbledon with injury, and was seeking to reach his fourth New York semi-final in five years.

Regardless of his opponent's current levels, for Shelton this was a victory that could prove seismic in front of a home crowd who passionately backed him throughout.

"It is incredible, I always say that this is the greatest stadium in the world," the 23-year-old said.

"I'm just hoping my best friend and sister don't have to be at work at 6am. It would be huge from their employers to let them have the day off."

The American number one is through to his third major semi-final, having lost to two of the game's heavyweights in Jannik Sinner at last year's Australian Open and Novak Djokovic in New York three years ago. Both went on to be crowned champions.

After ousting Alcaraz, Shelton is now the second-highest ranked player remaining in the draw after world number two Alexander Zverev.

It remains to be seen how Shelton will recover for the semi-final against Tiafoe, who completed a remarkable comeback from two sets and a break down to beat compatriot Alex Michelsen.

"For me, it's always about the people in the crowd - whether it's my coaches and my team, all of my family and friends," Shelton said.

"The city of New York that showed up tonight until 3am, that's what kept me going."

Sabalenka fights back to keep US Open defence alive

Osaka makes passionate defence of on-court outfits

A closely contested first set offered a hint of the momentum swings that would define the match.

Alcaraz edged the opener on a tie-break - but only after surrendering his advantage after breaking for a seemingly decisive 6-5 lead.

Shelton, however, was ruthless as Alcaraz's level dropped sharply and embarked on a run of nine unanswered games to claim the second set and take charge of the third.

Refusing to fold, Alcaraz launched his fourth-set revival by saving two break points and then breaking when Shelton missed a backhand.

Alcaraz appeared to be sick into his towel during a changeover, such was his level of physical exertion, but would break Shelton a second time as he earned a fifth set as the time approached 02:30.

Both players failed to take break-point opportunities before a match-deciding breaker swung back and forth.

Shelton led 3-1 and Alcaraz regained control at 5-3.

But the Spaniard's uncharacteristically high number of unforced errors - the second seed made 53 overall - ultimately cost him, as Shelton captured five of the next six points before seeing out victory in style with an ace.

'An opponent has to take advantage - and Shelton did'

The first sign that all was not well with Alcaraz came at the end of the first set.

His forehand was off, and his serve erratic. Some of the rallies were stunning, but he was playing carelessly at times, and sometimes seemed disengaged as his concentration fluctuated.

All of which can be expected of someone who was playing just his fifth singles match since April and a first against a top-10 player.

But the opponent has to take advantage - and Shelton did so superbly.

Shelton has previously had a miserable record against the very best, losing all 17 of his previous matches against top-three players.

The flashy left-hander played plenty of shots and sent down one serve at 149mph, but was excellent on return and disciplined in defence.

By the fourth and fifth sets, Alcaraz was locked in again but could not prevent Shelton closing out the win of his life.

articles.title: US Open: Ben Shelton beats Carlos Alcaraz in five-set thriller in latest-ever finish to US Open match at 3.33am
articles.summary: Ben Shelton clinches first-ever victory over top-three opponent as he beats Carlos Alcaraz to set up US Open semi-final showdown with Frances Tiafoe; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
The American prevailed 6-7 (5-7) 6-1 6-3 1-6 7-6 (10-7) over four hours and 28 minutes to reward a raucous Arthur Ashe Stadium crowd gripped until 3.33am in what was the latest-ever finish to a US Open match.

It marked Shelton's first career win over a top-three player, against which he had been 0-17 coming into the match.

Shelton will now play Frances Tiafoe in the final four after his fellow countryman's thrilling five-set victory over Alex Michelsen earlier in the evening.

"For me it's always about the people in the crowd, whether it's my coaches, team or friends and family, or the city of New York that showed up tonight until 3am with the USA chants, that's what kept me going and what got me this win," Shelton said on-court.

"It's incredible. This is the greatest sports city and greatest stadium in the world. I'm hoping my best friend and sister don't have to be at work at 6am.

"I'm so grateful, so blessed to be in front of you guys and share the court with Carlos is an absolute honour."

Shelton's victory means the United States is guaranteed representation in Sunday's men's final, with Andy Roddick the last American man to win a major title back in 2003.

It also spelled the end of Alcaraz's courageous return to the court having been out for more than four months with a wrist injury and initially been a doubt to compete in New York.

The seven-time major champion, playing his first tournament since April, was seen vomiting before the beginning of the final set, which culminated in a 10-point match-deciding tie-break.

"As I said before the tournament began, the expectation was to go there, compete... playing these kind of matches, for me being healthy," said Alcaraz. "It was close, it really was close. So I'm just a little bit disappointed, about, (not) getting the win at the end.

"But, I'm just happy, I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought. After the third set, physically I was really tired, but I found a way to push myself up, physically give an extra. In the fifth set

"I just started to feel better and better. I was playing against one of the... he is a beast. He's an unbelievable player. Powerful. He just managed how to play really, really well in every situation, so credit to him. I leave the court happy, I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed."

Shelton heads into his third Grand Slam semi-final having previously reached the final four of the 2023 US Open and the 2025 Australian Open.

Having lost the opening tie-break, the 23-year-old stormed to nine straight games on his way to dominant second and third sets. Back came Alcaraz to send it to a decider, where he would win four successive points to lead 5-3 in the tie-break before inviting Shelton to turn things around.

In true Shelton fashion, he iced the game with a serve of 146mph that Alcaraz failed to tame, bringing the New York crowd to their feet.

"I remember, the last tiebreak that I played was in Paris," recalled Alcaraz. "It was an unbelievable game that I played in that moment. This time, when you are trying to fight and trying to overcome all the problems you might have - physically, tired a lot, obviously when he's serving, he puts a lot of pressure on you.

"You're thinking about, trying to put the return in, and it's unknown if you're going to play the point or he's going to get a free point with the serve. I think in these moments he takes a lot of advantage with serve, but not any excuse, but I would say it's an important weapon in these moments."

Tiafoe reaches US Open semis in thrilling fightback

Frances Tiafoe recovered from two sets down and ‌erased a 0-3 deficit in the fifth set to beat American compatriot Alex Michelsen 5-7 3-6 7-5 6-3 7-6 (10-6), reaching the semi-finals for a third time.

The 11th seed ​appeared to have lost all the magic of his early campaign before claiming the momentum in the third set and clinching ​it with a forehand winner to the deafening cheers of ‌the fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Michelsen had flown under the radar in his deepest major run but ​earned respect on the biggest stage of American tennis with 21 aces, and Tiafoe cut his own celebration short to comfort the 22-year-old in an emotional ​embrace.

"I hope he gets tight," Tiafoe said of his mindset at 4-5 down in the third set. "He gave me some gifts, a couple of double faults there.

"But then I slowly started to get my rhythm there, snuck out the third set and slowly started playing better and better.

"He is a hell of a player. He should've easily won today, so shout out Alex Michelsen."

Tiafoe joined Andre Agassi as the only American men to reach three US Open semi-finals in this century and will return to the top 10 for the first time in three years in the rankings.

"Everyone was sleeping in the first couple of hours and I was asleep with you all," Tiafoe joked following his win.

"As it went along, the energy was incredible, as always. Thank you [to the crowd] for being there for me. I really appreciate that."

"You can't help but feel sorry for Alex Michelsen considering how close he was and we all know Frances is a fan favourite in this situation.

"The tears started coming from Michelsen. It was like a punch in the gut for me and I don't even know him.

"Having been in these situations when you're so close to the finishing line and you know it's on your racket, I think that's the worst feeling. You know that you kind of did choke a little bit. That's the absolute worst.

"Brutal day for him but you have to tip your cap to Frances for turning that match around."

The titanic quarterfinal lasted four hours and 28 minutes, eventually ending at 3:33 a.m. local time in New York’s Arthur Ashe Stadium. It all appeared to be going to plan for Alcaraz after he won the first-set tiebreak, but Shelton stormed back in the next two sets to take a 2-1 lead in the match. But the Spaniard won the fourth set to take the contest to a deciding set that went the distance. With thousands of fans sticking around to watch the epic, Shelton was buoyed by the home support and found the energy to edge the match-deciding tiebreak and win the record-breaking quarterfinal in five sets – 6-7(5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6(7). “I mean, it’s incredible,” Shelton said after securing the win with a monster 146-mph serve. “I always say this is the greatest sports city in the world, the greatest stadium in the world.” He added: “For me, it’s always about the people in the crowd. articles.summary: Reigning U.S. Open champion Carlos Alcaraz was upset 6-7 (5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (7), in the quarterfinals of the 2026 U.S. Open at Arthur Ashe Stadium in Queens, New York, on Tuesday night.
articles.body:
Reigning U.S. Open champion Carlos Alcaraz was upset 6-7 (5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (7), in the quarterfinals of the 2026 U.S. Open at Arthur Ashe Stadium in Queens, New York, on Tuesday night.

Following a late start, the match poured over into the wee hours of Wednesday morning, and it came to an end about four-and-a-half hours after it started, concluding at 3:33 a.m. ET, per ESPN .

For the eighth-seeded Shelton, it was arguably the biggest win of his career, as he took down the No. 2 seed and No. 3 player in the world to reach his third Grand Slam semifinal.

A career Grand Slam winner, the 23-year-old Alcaraz made his long-awaited return at the U.S. Open after missing both the French Open and Wimbledon with a wrist injury.

Despite the long layoff, he was considered the odds-on favorite, especially with world No. 1 Jannik Sinner not playing in the tournament due to a knee ailment.

Alcaraz ran into the hard-serving Shelton in the quarters, though, and he did so on Shelton's home soil.

Seemingly feeding off the atmosphere, Shelton was the better player on Tuesday night, breaking Alcaraz's serve five times compared to the three breaks Alcaraz got on him.

On top of that, Shelton committed only 35 unforced errors over the course of the five-set match, whereas Alcaraz made an uncharacteristic 53 unforced errors.

With No. 11 Frances Tiafoe beating fellow American Alex Michelsen earlier Tuesday, it means an American player is guaranteed to play in the U.S. Open men's singles final.

Either Shelton or Tiafoe will become the first American man to reach a Grand Slam singles final since Taylor Fritz at the 2024 U.S. Open. Before that, Andy Roddick was the last American man to make it to a Grand Slam singles final at Wimbledon 2009.

Roddick is also the most recent American men's Grand Slam singles champion, winning the U.S. Open back in 2003.

After squeaking past Alcaraz, Shelton is favored to take down Tiafoe and reach his first Grand Slam singles final where he would meet one of top-seeded Alexander Zverev, No. 28 Alexander Blockx, Botic van de Zandschulp or Karen Khachanov.

Following his marathon victory over Alcaraz, Shelton is scheduled to be back in action Friday when he and Tiafoe determine which American will go on to play for the U.S. Open title.

articles.title: A $15 billion tennis match? How Pegula and Navarro turned a US Open clash into a 'battle of the billionaires' that dwarfed Djokovic, Federer and Nadal’s combined wealth
articles.summary: Tennis News: The US Open produced an unusual storyline even before Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro walked onto Arthur Ashe Stadium.This was not just an all-America.
articles.body: The US Open produced an unusual storyline even before Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro walked onto Arthur Ashe Stadium.This was not just an all-American quarter-final between two of the country's leading tennis players. It was a meeting between two women whose families have amassed fortunes running into billions of dollars, turning their US Open clash into what fans quickly dubbed the “Battle of the Billionaires.”When the numbers were put together, the combined estimated wealth of the Pegula and Navarro families was reported at around $15 billion. And while the money had nothing to do with what happened once the match began, it certainly added a fascinating subplot to one of the biggest matches of the US Open.Pegula wins the 'Battle of the Billionaires'The sporting contest ultimately belonged to Pegula. The third-seeded American recovered from losing the opening set to beat 26th seed Navarro 3-6, 6-4, 6-3, booking her place in the US Open semi-finals for the third consecutive year. She will face world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka in the last four.For Navarro, it was another impressive run in New York after she reached the semi-finals at the 2024 US Open.The Pegula family fortuneJessica Pegula is the daughter of Terry Pegula, the billionaire businessman who owns the NFL's Buffalo Bills and NHL's Buffalo Sabres. Forbes' current estimate cited in reports puts Terry Pegula's fortune at around $11.8 billion. His wealth was originally built in the energy sector before he made major investments in professional sports.Jessica, however, has carved out her own identity in professional tennis. The 32-year-old is a former US Open finalist, has won multiple WTA titles and has established herself as one of the most consistent players on the women's tour. She entered this year's tournament as the No. 3 seed and was already a two-time US Open semi-finalist before beating Navarro.The Navarro family fortuneAcross the net was Emma Navarro, daughter of businessman Ben Navarro, founder of Sherman Financial Group. Ben Navarro's fortune has been estimated at around $3.2 billion. His business interests extend beyond finance and into tennis itself, with the family investing heavily in the sport, including ownership of major tournaments such as the Cincinnati Open and Charleston Open.Emma has also established herself as a serious force on court. She reached the US Open semi-finals in 2024, climbed as high as No. 8 in the world and returned to the quarter-finals in New York this year after an impressive run through the draw.$15 billion vs tennis' big threeThe eye-catching comparison that caught social media's attention was the claim by the fans that the two families' combined wealth, around $15 billion, dwarfs the estimated combined fortunes of tennis legends Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal.That comparison needs a little context.The Pegula and Navarro figures refer largely to family wealth, principally that of their billionaire fathers. The Djokovic, Federer and Nadal figures generally refer to the players' own accumulated wealth from prize money, endorsements, investments and businesses. So it is not a like-for-like financial comparison.Federer became tennis’ first billionaire according to Forbes, although his fortune later slipped below $1 billion following a fall in the value of his stake in sportswear company On.Nadal, meanwhile, earned more than $550 million in career pretax earnings from prize money, endorsements and other business ventures, according to Forbes, while Djokovic has earned a record $195 million in ATP prize money alone.Still, the sheer size of the number made the quarter-final an irresistible talking point online.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Who are Qinwen Zheng’s parents? Meet Zheng Jianping and Deng Fang, the people behind her tennis journey
articles.summary: International Sports News: Qinwen Zheng’s rise in tennis has been closely linked to the support of her parents, Zheng Jianping and Deng Fang. The Chinese star was born in Shiyan.
articles.body: Qinwen Zheng’s rise in tennis has been closely linked to the support of her parents, Zheng Jianping and Deng Fang. The Chinese star was born in Shiyan, Hubei, and started playing sports as a young child before tennis became her main focus. Her parents soon realized that she had the talent and drive to go further. From changing cities for better coaching to making major personal sacrifices, they played a big role in her journey.Who are Qinwen Zheng’s parents, Zheng Jianping and Deng Fang?Qinwen’s father, Zheng Jianping, had a sporting background of his own. He competed in track and field events in Hubei and was part of the province’s second-level track team during his high school years. After leaving sports, he moved into business and later ran an auto parts company in Shiyan that dealt with cars, steel and construction materials.His own experience in sports helped him understand the hard work needed to compete at a high level. When Qinwen was young, Jianping encouraged her to try different sports. A moment when she chose to run instead of taking a ride in the family car helped him notice how much she enjoyed physical activity. Tennis eventually became the sport she wanted to pursue.Qinwen’s mother, Deng Fang, came from a very different work background. She studied railway transport and worked at railway stations in Hubei, including jobs involving ticket sales. Her role later changed when Qinwen’s tennis career became more demanding. Deng left her job so she could spend more time with her daughter and take care of her during training and travel.The two parents supported Qinwen in different ways. Her father focused heavily on her tennis development and the decisions around her career, while her mother handled much of the daily care. Qinwen has spoken about how important both parents have been to her success.Qinwen Zheng’s tennis journey and how her parents supported herQinwen was born on October 8, 2002, in Shiyan, Hubei. She began playing tennis locally when she was six, but her parents soon understood that she would need better coaching to develop properly. When she was eight, the family moved her to Wuhan, around 200 kilometers away, where she trained for several years.Her next move was to Beijing, where she received more advanced training. Then, at 17, Qinwen moved to Barcelona with her mother to continue her development and compete in Europe. By then, tennis had become a full-time commitment, and her family had built their lives around giving her the best chance to succeed.That path also came with a major financial cost. Qinwen has said her father made huge sacrifices to keep paying for her career, including selling the family home. Some reports have put the total amount spent on her development at around 20 million yuan, although that figure has not been independently confirmed.Deng’s sacrifice was just as important in a different way. After leaving her railway job, she stayed close to Qinwen and helped manage the everyday parts of her life, from meals and travel to making sure she had support away from the court.Qinwen has never hidden how much she values what her parents did for her. After winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, she credited them for helping her reach that level. Their approach was demanding, but it gave her the chance to build a career on her own terms.That support can still be seen in Qinwen’s attitude on court. Her ability to keep fighting when a match looks almost lost has become one of her biggest strengths. Behind that mindset is a childhood shaped by constant training, difficult moves and parents who were willing to change their own lives to help her chase a much bigger dream.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: The US Open — and Ben Shelton — is putting on a great show. But why is it happening at 3:33 a.m.?
articles.summary: Shelton took down 7-time major winner Carlos Alcaraz, but was anyone awake to watch?
articles.body:
When Ben Shelton delivered the 146 mile per hour ace that f inally defeated Carlos Alcaraz to reach the US Open semifinals , it was arguably the most significant moment for American men's tennis in many years.

Though Shelton's stunning win over the seven-time major champion ensures the U.S. TV audience will be highly engaged for Sunday's final since either Shelton or fellow American Frances Tiafoe will be there, the quarterfinal classic that unfolded from late Tuesday night into Wednesday morning was a massive missed opportunity for tennis.

If the USTA's mission is to truly grow interest and participation in tennis across the country, you cannot just accept that it's "part of the sport" for the marquee match of the biggest American tournament, pitting two of the most charismatic and popular players against each other, to start just after 11 p.m. on a weeknight.

Alcaraz and Shelton put on a show — a breathtaking display of athleticism, skill and stage presence. It was the kind of match that makes the sport look fun and cool, that can inspire kids to ask their parents about starting tennis lessons or maybe help that elite young athlete decide he wants to be the next Shelton rather than the next Lamar Jackson.

That match has to be in prime time, in every living room in America that has sports on TV. It cannot happen when most of the country is asleep.

In fact, it ended so late that they didn't even bother bringing in Shelton for a traditional press conference, relegating him to discuss the biggest win of his life with reporters asking only a couple of questions outside the locker room.

"That was a war, epic match, so physical," Shelton said. "Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old. It's always fun being on the court against him. It's ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes. But, yeah, the most enjoyable match that I've had in my career, for sure."

It's hard to put your finger on it, but there's something culturally significant happening around tennis these days. Lots of new people started playing during the COVID-19 pandemic, influencers are popping up at big events, there's a huge market for tennis documentaries these days on Netflix and Amazon Prime and it's getting really hard ( and expensive ) to land a ticket to any of the Grand Slams. More and more star athletes in the big mainstream sports are showing up at matches and talking about tennis on social media because they appreciate how electric the sport is when you've got stars like Alcaraz and Shelton playing on the big stage.

Instead, tennis does a lot of shrugging its shoulders.

Each of the four Grand Slams has its own unique scheduling problems, but across the board, it's undeniable that things are getting worse.

The US Open has always had some really late matches, and in some ways, it has become part of the tournament's lore. It's almost a badge of honor to say "I was there" for the five-setter that finishes well after midnight.

But it's not supposed to be a nightly occurrence. And at this year's tournament, it's happening more often than not. A sporting event finishing after 1 a.m. needs to be an outlier, not the norm. And at some point, one of the big stakeholders in tennis needs to admit that it's bad for fans, it's bad for the tournament's TV partners, it's bad for tournament employees, and most of all, it's bad for the players because a match is not done when it ends. You're talking hours of rehab, refueling and cool-down before they even think about getting to bed.

This isn't what spectator sports are supposed to be.

That doesn't mean the solutions are easy. And the biggest impediment to finding one is that tennis is a sport without a clock.

The Arthur Ashe Stadium schedule Tuesday was normal, starting at 11:30 with women's No. 1 seed Aryna Sabalenka. But she took 2 hours, 22 minutes to beat Linda Noskova, which was followed by Tiafoe's epic 4-hour, 39-minute win over Alex Michelsen in a fifth-set tiebreaker.

As a result, the day session for those matches spilled into the 7 p.m. hour, which is when the night session was supposed to start. But because it's a different ticket, they had to clear the stadium after the Tiafoe match before even beginning the Jessica Pegula-Emma Navarro match at 8:20 p.m. And because that match went three sets and took 2 hours, 21 minutes, everything went haywire.

Even if the USTA decided that this isn't acceptable, what could they do about it? It's easy to say they should just move one of the matches to another court, but the second-biggest court at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center holds roughly 10,000 fewer people than Ashe and doesn't have luxury suites. You'd literally be cutting the legs out from thousands of ticket-buyers, and even though the USTA has become a massively greedy organization, it's hard to say they should just punt on millions of dollars in revenue.

Perhaps they could reimagine the schedule and follow the French Open model, where there's just one night match starting at 8 p.m.

But at the French, they've decided that match nearly always needs to be a men's match because best-of-five theoretically gives ticket-buyers more tennis to watch than a best-of-three women's match. As a result, the French Open becomes the center of an annual media circus where they get accused of sexism. And, of course, having one standalone match always carries the risk of a blowout or someone getting injured, and it's an unsatisfying experience for everyone.

Something else the tournament should probably consider is whether they can do anything in the future to speed up the court. Tournaments can manipulate the court surface when it's being built for balls to bounce lower and shoot through the court, rewarding bigger shots and faster serves. Players these days are bigger and stronger and cover more court than ever, while the surfaces are getting slower and balls are bouncing higher. That's a natural recipe for long rallies and longer matches.

Ultimately, though, tennis may need to think about the best-of-five format. Yes, it's one of the sport's sacred cows and a true separator of good vs. great. But it also causes a ton of scheduling problems at the Slams. Maybe there's a middle ground where, if a match goes two sets each, you play a 10-point tiebreaker instead of a fifth.

Any decision like that, though, needs to be carefully considered because there is just so much history wrapped up in best-of-five.

"I think for the men's we should stick with three out of five," Tiafoe said. "I don't know where the conversation is going, what people are leaning to. Everyone is going to have an opinion. We've seen so many epics in five-setters. Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not. There's a lot of times where I'm up two sets to love, I would love to shake hands and go home. But it's tennis, man.

"I grew up watching so many incredible five-setters. Novak-Rafa, Federer-Rafa, epic five-setters that go on for hours and hours. That's the history of the game. (If) you do that, I feel like your Slam doesn't mean as much personally if you get it done in a two-out-of-three format."

A lot of people agree with Tiafoe. But it's also a valid question whether, in 2026, any sporting event should last five hours.

It's a real conundrum. We should all be able to agree, though, that an otherwise magnificent US Open is not getting the maximum benefit from all this great tennis because too many of us are asleep when it happens. Ending a sporting event continually after 2 a.m. is not the answer.

articles.title: Why the best match of the US Open finished after 3 a.m. – and how it could affect Ben Shelton in the semis
articles.summary: After Ben Shelton’s time-zone-spanning quarterfinal against Carlos Alcaraz finished at 3:33 a.m. in New York Wednesday morning, the annual conversation of match scheduling at the US Open has kicked back up again.
articles.body: After Ben Shelton’s time-zone-spanning quarterfinal against Carlos Alcaraz finished at 3:33 a.m. in New York Wednesday morning, the annual conversation of match scheduling at the US Open has kicked back up again. Despite how bizarre it was to see the two players still battling it out in the early hours, the scene was not one alien to this year’s tournament. Over the years, titanic night sessions have become synonymous with the US Open. To some, they are exactly what makes the grand slam so special. But for others, namely the players and fans with actual tickets, it’s becoming an unsustainable trend that pushes athletes to their absolute limits and leads to empty stands for some of the biggest matches. So why are the US Open matches finishing so late and what, if anything, can be done about it? Why so late? While late finishes have become commonplace at the US Open, this year has been particularly bad. Shelton’s quarterfinal win was the latest end to a day in the tournament’s history, not starting until past 11 p.m. ET, meaning many fans had to leave before the match even started. And, in many ways, this was predictable. The schedule at the US Open (and at two of the other three grand slams) is split into two – a day and night session – which basically allows organizers to sell two batches of tickets for the courts, essentially doubling the possible revenue. The most high-profile matches involving the world’s best players are often saved for the evenings, allowing for more lucrative TV deals at primetime slots for fans finishing work to watch. But with the late session in Flushing Meadows not starting until 7 p.m. ET and with no curfew in place – unlike the 11 p.m. cut off at Wimbledon – it’s no surprise that matches regularly tick past midnight. In the case of last night, it was simply the perfect storm. Two matches before Shelton’s quarterfinal were marathons that went the distance, which pushed back the start of the night session by 30 minutes. But even though Wednesday morning was a bit extreme, late finishes are still very frequent and currently unavoidable with the current setup. “This is not sustainable,” 18-time grand slam singles champion Martina Navratilova warned on X earlier this tournament, after a swathe of late finishes. “That’s simply too late to play tennis,” former tennis champion Boris Becker replied. What do the players say? There is no doubt that epic night sessions can help create electric memories. But at what cost? After all, it’s clear the players are struggling with the current schedule. After an already packed calendar throughout the season, stars are turning up tired to the US Open and then being asked to push their bodies to the limits at ungodly hours in front of dwindling crowds. Sleep schedules, meal times and warmups are all impacted by the ticking clock. And it’s not as though players go straight home after the match ends. Shelton and Alcaraz would have had press responsibilities to perform, needed to warm down properly and eat and drink something to aid in their recovery. How can that not impact Shelton ahead of his match against Frances Tiafoe in the final four on Friday? “When you finish late, the next day shifts a lot,” women’s star Aryna Sabalenka said earlier in the tournament. “Like, you still need to get your hours of sleep, so you start later. You just can really mess up your schedule.” Sabalenka is not alone; Venus Williams also said it was “not ideal” that her match against Sofia Kenin last week didn’t start until past midnight. “I think it wasn’t great for either of us, so I think we both tried our best,” she said. “Yeah, I just don’t know any other sport where you have to start that late. I definitely think there’s room for improvement there.” Will things change? To combat late finishes, the simplest thing to do would surely be to start earlier, right? But that’s more complicated than you might think. Shifting things earlier in the day might lead to less revenue from TV deals and could make it hard for fans to travel to Flushing Meadows through New York’s infamous rush hour. “Tuesday was one of the most extraordinary days of tennis the US Open has ever seen. While we remain astonished by the incredible competition that played out on the court in Arthur Ashe Stadium – four matches that went a maximum of 16 sets and featured three final-set tiebreaks – we acknowledge that we must evaluate all scheduling options in the future,” said Brendan McIntyre, head of US Open communications. “The focus and attention must remain on these remarkable athletes and their amazing performances rather than on the finishing time.” Ironically, tournament director Eric Butorac spoke to ESPN earlier this month and said scheduling matches was like a “jigsaw puzzle” and was his favorite part of the job. “In New York, it would be a challenge to start before 7 p.m. Could we do 6?” he pondered. “It’s something we’re going to address every year.” Notably, though, he said 7 p.m. still felt like the “right time” for now.

articles.summary: La ciudad italiana releva a Riad (Arabia Saudí) como ubicación del Masters de los jóvenes en 2026
articles.body: La ATP ha anunciado que Reggio Calabria será la sede de las Next Gen ATP Finals de 2026, lo que supone el regreso del torneo a Italia, país donde se celebró por primera vez en 2017. El Masters de los mejores jóvenes se había celebrado inicialmente en Milán y en 2023 voló a Riad (Arabia Saudí). El torneo se jugará del 9 al 16 de diciembre y tendrá una bolsa en premios de dos millones de dólares. El estadounidense Learner Tien fue el último campeón en un certamen en el que también estuvieron los madrileños Rafa Jódar y Martín Landaluce. Por edad, tanto Jódar como Landaluce pueden repetir presencia, no en vano son el número 1 y 3, respectivamente en la Raca sub'20. El brasileño Joao Fonseca se cuela entre los dos. Cabe recordar que Turín tomó el relevó de Londres como ubicación de las ATP Finals. Después de cinco exitosas ediciones se ha renovado la apuesta por la localidad del Piamonte hasta 2027. En tierras italianas también se celebran desde el año pasado las finales de la Copa Davis en Bolonia. El acuerdo entre la federación italiana y la ITF es por tres campañas.

articles.standfirst: La kazaja remonta un set a la china Zheng y relevará a Sabalenka el próximo lunes en lo más alto de la WTA
articles.summary: La kazaja remonta un set a la china Zheng y relevará a Sabalenka el próximo lunes en lo más alto de la WTA
articles.body: Elena Rybakina, de 27 años, recordará toda su vida el 9 de septiembre de 2026. La kazaja se ha convertido en la trigésima tenista que asciende a lo más alto del ranking femenino tras derrotar este miércoles a Qinwen Zheng, por 3-6, 6-1 y 6-4, y acceder así a las semifinales del US Open. Las 99 semanas de número 1 de Aryna Sabalenka tocarán a su fin el próximo lunes cuando se actualice de manera oficial la clasificación mundial. Zheng, la 121 al inicio del certamen y procedente de la previa, vendió cara la derrota. La pupila de Pere Riba ha recuperado en las pistas de Flushing Meadows el nivel que la condujo a la medalla de oro en los pasado Juegos Olímpicos de París y a disputar la final del Open de Australia 2024. Rybakina, con su habitual cara de póker, le fue poco a poco comiendo terreno a su rival. Lejos quedan las dudas por la lesión en el talón en Cincinnati y que casi la dejan fuera del cuarto grande del calendario. Los 8.681 puntos que suma Elena en su casillero la hacen inalcanzable tanto para Sabalenka como para Jessica Pegula y Coco Gauff. Las tres tenían posibilidades matemáticas de salir de Nueva York como líderes del circuito.

articles.title: US Open: Elena Rybakina ends Qinwen Zheng's run, becomes new women's No. 1 with win in quarterfinal
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina is a step closer to winning her first-ever US Open title.
articles.body:
There was a lot at stake for Elena Rybakina during her quarterfinal match against Qinwen Zheng on Wednesday. With a victory, Rybakina would not only move a step closer to winning her first US Open, she would also assume the title of the No. 1 ranked women's player in the sport.

Well, move over Aryna Sabalenka, because you've been dethroned. Rybakina advanced Wednesday, beating Zheng in three sets (3-6, 6-1, 6-4) to keep her US Open title hopes alive and become the top-ranked women's player in the world.

Sabalenka had previously held the No. 1 rank for the past 99 weeks. But some earlier-than-expected exits, combined with improved play from Rybakina, put that position in limbo heading into Wednesday. All Rybakina needed was a win over Zheng to take the top spot. It was a hard-fought match, but Rybakina did it.

It marks the first time in her career Rybakina has been ranked No. 1.

It also marks the furthest Rybakina has ever advanced at the US Open. Her previous high came last year, when she reached the fourth round of the event before falling.

Typically, the US Open has proven to be Rybakina's most difficult Grand Slam. Entering play Wednesday, she had won just 57 percent of her matches at the event.

The win not only solidifies Rybakina's status as the top woman in the sport right now but sets her up to potentially capture her third Grand Slam win. Rybakina has already won Wimbledon and the Australian Open. A win at the US Open would leave the French Open as the only Grand Slam she's yet to conquer.

Getting there won't be easy. After narrowly defeating Zheng on Wednesday, Rybakina is guaranteed to take on some of the highest ranked women the rest of the way, as many of the favorites on the women's side advanced to the quarterfinals.

As her new No. 1 ranking suggests, Rybakina should be up for any challenge at this point … even if she manages to trail early.

Qinwen Zheng outlasts Elena Rybakina in first set

That's exactly what happened Wednesday, as Rybakina and Zheng got off to an exciting start, trading the first seven games in the first set. In Game 8, Zheng finally broke Rybakina to take a 5-3 lead. Rybakina nearly did the same in the ninth game, taking three of the first four points in the game. But Zheng battled back, with the game eventually getting the deuce.

From there, Rybakina and Zheng reached an advantage a combined seven times before Zheng was finally able to close out the game. In doing so, she took the first set 6-3.

Both players appeared to be trying hard for aces in the first set, as neither managed a first serve percentage above 50. Zheng was more successful on that front, notching four aces against Rybakina's one in the set.

Elena Rybakina hits her stride in second set

It was a much different story in the second set. Rybakina got a better handle on her serve, while Zheng often failed to put her first attempt in play. During the set, Rybakina was successful on 58 percent of her first-serve attempts. Zheng clocked in at 38 percent. While it wasn't a flawless game from Rybakina — who had more unforced errors and two double faults — it didn't look that way on paper.

Rybakina cruised to a 6-1 win in the second set, breaking Zheng twice to pick up the victory and send the match to a third set.

After a tense final set, Rybakina pulls out the win

Both players locked in during the final set. With both consistently getting their first-serve attempts in, Rybakina and Zheng traded the first eight games in the set.

It wasn't until the ninth game that Rybakina finally broke Zheng. That set up a 10th game in which Rybakina would serve with the match potentially on the line.

She got the job done, finally dispatching Zheng — who has proven to be a thorn in the side of many higher-ranked opponents at the event — and moving to the semifinals.

Even with the loss, Zheng proved she's nearly back to form after battling injuries early in 2026. After first-round exits at both the French Open and Wimbledon, Zheng showed the form that allowed her to take gold at the 2024 Olympics. If she can retain that, Zheng should shoot back up the rankings after injuries resulted in her fall.

For Rybakina, she can keep her eyes on the prize. There's no better way to follow up her coronation than to go out and win a Grand Slam. If she can do that, she'll leave no doubt she deserves to be No. 1.

articles.title: Elena Rybakina moves to No. 1 in the women’s rankings after reaching US Open semifinals
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina is headed to the US Open semifinals and to the top of the women’s tennis rankings.
articles.body: Elena Rybakina is headed to the US Open semifinals and to the top of the women’s tennis rankings. Rybakina edged Zheng Qinwen 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 on Wednesday, guaranteeing she will become No. 1 in the WTA rankings. The Australian Open champion will face No. 4 Coco Gauff or No. 5 Mirra Andreeva on Thursday. Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka faces No. 3 Jessica Pegula in the other semifinal. But no matter what happens in the remaining matches, Rybakina will end Sabalenka’s 99-week stay at No. 1 when the new rankings are released Monday. “It’s just a number right now and of course I’m in the semis and my goal is to win the tournament,” Rybakina said. Zheng, the 2024 Olympic gold medalist from China, had to come through the qualifying tournament just to make the main draw after elbow surgery dropped her down the rankings to her current place of No. 121. Once ranked No. 4, she is guaranteed to move back into the top 60. She made a dramatic run to the quarterfinals, erasing a 5-0 deficit in the third set against Madison Keys in the third round and then climbing out of another 5-0 hole in the first set in her fourth-round victory over No. 8-seed Iga Swiatek. But a double fault gave her opponent a 5-4 lead in the third set and Rybakina served it out to reach the US Open semifinals for the first time.
